idiom_name: null reference or empty anonymous implementation; Mockito only as a fallback
implementation_notes: Java has no non-null type, so the placeholder is almost always null - both for the parameter itself and for a collaborator the constructor merely stores. Where a null-hostile API or a nullness annotation processor forbids null (JSpecify, @NonNull), the one-line anonymous implementation new Collaborator() {...} or an empty test-local class is the dummy, and for a wide interface Mockito's mock(Foo.class) fabricates one; that mock is loose by default, answers arbitrary calls with defaults and stops being a dummy the moment it is used. Unused parameters need no annotation on the callee side, and the compiler does not warn about them. A null placeholder enforces the assumption at the first call with a NullPointerException, which is a blunt but immediate signal.
pitfalls: A row of bare nulls compiles and reads ambiguously - overload resolution can even pick a different constructor than intended - so name the position in a comment or route construction through a small test factory.
Mockito's mock(Foo.class) is loose: an unconfigured mock returns defaults for every member, so a path that starts reading the placeholder stays green with fabricated data instead of failing.
A null placeholder fails on the first method call, which may be on another thread or after the assertions, leaving a NullPointerException in a stack frame that never mentions the dummy.
